analogy.p: Imagine a giant keyboard that runs from the lowest rumble at the left to the highest squeak at the right, with **no gaps between keys**. The left end is **radio waves** (long, slow wobbles), the middle holds one tiny group of keys that your eyes happen to hear, **visible light**, and the right end is **gamma rays** (short, extremely rapid wobbles). Every key plays at the **same speed through space**, but the keys on the right carry **much more energy** and can break things. The analogy breaks down because the EM spectrum is not sound: EM waves are **transverse** and need **no medium**, and the real range is far wider than any piano.
analogy.t: A radio dial across a very wide piano

bullets: EM waves are **transverse**; they **transfer energy** from a **source** to an **absorber**.
The groups form a **continuous spectrum** (no gaps); the boundaries between groups are approximate.
Order (long wavelength to short): **radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma**.
All EM waves travel at the **same speed in a vacuum (and approximately in air): 3.0 x 10^8 m/s**.
The **eye detects only visible light**.
Different substances **absorb, transmit, refract or reflect** EM waves depending on the **wavelength**.
Uses, dangers and the production of radio waves are separate spec points; here you must secure the **properties and the order**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 (4.6 Waves) expects you to know that **electromagnetic (EM) waves are transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber**. They form a **continuous spectrum**, and every type travels at the **same speed through a vacuum (space) or air**. The waves are grouped by **wavelength and frequency**, and from **long wavelength to short wavelength** (or **low frequency to high frequency**) the groups are: **radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays**. You also need to know that **our eyes only detect visible light**, so we detect only a limited range of EM waves, and that **different substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect EM waves in ways that vary with wavelength**.

bullets: **Transverse:** the oscillations are **perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer.
**No medium needed**, so they travel through space, unlike sound (longitudinal, needs particles).
They **transfer energy**, not matter: the absorber gains energy (for example the internal energy of skin increases).
Each wave has a **wavelength** (distance between two crests), a **frequency** (waves per second, in Hz) and an **amplitude** (maximum displacement from the rest position).
Because they are transverse, EM waves can show **polarisation** (extra detail, not required).
EM waves can be **reflected, refracted, absorbed and transmitted**, like other waves.
The **source** is where the energy comes from; the **absorber** is where it ends up: this phrase is in the specification, so use it.
core.p: An EM wave is a **transverse wave** in which **electric and magnetic fields** vibrate at right angles to each other and to the direction the wave is travelling. Unlike sound or water waves, EM waves **do not need a medium**: they can travel through a **vacuum**, which is why light and other radiation reach us from the Sun across empty space. Like all waves, they **transfer energy without transferring matter**: energy leaves a **source** (for example a hot filament) and is delivered to an **absorber** (for example your skin or an aerial), which heats up or is affected in some other way.

bullets: **Longest wavelength / lowest frequency:** radio waves.
**Shortest wavelength / highest frequency:** gamma rays.
Within **visible light**, **red** has the longest wavelength (about 700 nm) and **violet** the shortest (about 400 nm), so the order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
**Wavelength and frequency are inversely related:** if wavelength gets **shorter**, frequency gets **higher** (because c is fixed).
The groups are defined by **how they behave and how they are made**, not just by a sharp wavelength.
In Paper 2 you may be asked to **place the groups in order** or say which has a **higher frequency** than another.
The spectrum is **continuous**, so there are **no gaps** between the groups.
core.h: The continuous spectrum and its order
core.p: The **electromagnetic spectrum** is the whole family of EM waves arranged by wavelength or frequency. It is called **continuous** because there are no gaps: one type blends into the next, so the boundaries drawn on diagrams are not exact and some ranges (for example X-rays and gamma rays) **overlap**. The seven groups, from **longest wavelength / lowest frequency** to **shortest wavelength / highest frequency**, are **radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays**. A memory aid is **'Rabbits Mate In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens'** (Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma).

bullets: **Radio waves:** from about 0.1 m to many kilometres (long wavelength, lowest frequencies).
**Microwaves:** roughly 1 mm to 10 cm.
**Infrared:** roughly 700 nm up to 1 mm.
**Visible light:** about **400 nm to 700 nm** (4 x 10^-7 m to 7 x 10^-7 m), frequencies about **4.3 x 10^14 to 7.5 x 10^14 Hz**.
**Ultraviolet:** roughly 10 nm to 400 nm.
**X-rays:** roughly 10^-11 m to 10^-8 m; **gamma rays:** shorter than about 10^-11 m (the ranges overlap).
1 nm = 10^-9 m, so 700 nm = 7.0 x 10^-7 m: practise converting to **standard form**.
Wavelengths shrink as you go **up the spectrum**; frequencies and energies rise.
core.p: The wavelengths of EM waves cover an enormous range, from **kilometres for long radio waves to less than the size of an atomic nucleus for gamma rays**. You do not need to learn exact boundaries for the exam, but you should know the **order of magnitude** and that visible light is only a **tiny slice** in the middle. Because the speed is the same, the shortest wavelengths have the highest frequencies. For instance, red light of wavelength 700 nm has a frequency of about 4.3 x 10^14 Hz, while violet light of wavelength 400 nm has a frequency of about 7.5 x 10^14 Hz.

bullets: **c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s** in a vacuum (and nearly the same in air).
**wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m)**, so **frequency = speed ÷ wavelength** and **wavelength = speed ÷ frequency**.
If **frequency doubles**, **wavelength halves** (for the same speed).
**Distance = speed x time** is used for light-time questions: the Sun is about 1.5 x 10^11 m away, so light takes about 500 s (8.3 minutes) to reach us.
In a **vacuum** all EM waves have the **same speed**; in **materials** the speed is **lower** and can depend on wavelength (which is why a prism splits white light).
Common unit slips: **MHz = 10^6 Hz**, **GHz = 10^9 Hz**, **km = 10^3 m**, **nm = 10^-9 m**.
Always write the **equation, substitution, answer and unit**.
core.h: One speed in a vacuum, and the wave equation
core.p: All EM waves travel at the **same speed through a vacuum**, about **3.0 x 10^8 m/s** (300 million metres per second), and this is also very close to the speed in **air**. This speed is often given the symbol **c**. Since all types share one speed, the **wave equation** v = f x λ becomes **c = f x λ**, so a **higher frequency means a shorter wavelength**. The speed in other materials is **lower**: for example, light travels at about 2.0 x 10^8 m/s in glass.

bullets: **Higher frequency = more energy** carried by the radiation (and shorter wavelength).
**Ionising:** the **higher-frequency** part of UV, plus **X-rays and gamma rays**.
Ionising radiation can **damage cells**, cause **gene mutations** and may lead to **cancer**.
**Non-ionising:** radio, microwave, infrared and visible light (mainly cause **heating**, although very intense sources can also be harmful).
**Ultraviolet** can cause **skin ageing and an increased risk of skin cancer**.
**X-rays and gamma rays** are **ionising** and can cause **mutation of genes** and cancer.
The risk depends on the **type of radiation** and the **size of the dose** (radiation dose is measured in **sieverts, Sv**; 1000 millisieverts = 1 sievert).
core.p: As you go **up the spectrum** from radio to gamma, **frequency increases**, wavelength decreases and each wave carries **more energy**. This is why the **highest-frequency waves (ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays)** are the most dangerous: they carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms or molecules (**ionisation**) and can damage cells and DNA. These are called **ionising radiation**. Lower-frequency waves such as radio and microwaves have much less energy per wave and mainly cause heating when absorbed. The details of hazards are covered in the uses and dangers topic, but the link between **frequency and energy** is a key idea.

bullets: The eye detects **only visible light**, a **limited range** of EM waves.
**Red** has the **longest** wavelength; **violet** the **shortest** within visible light.
**White light** is a mix of colours; a **prism** disperses it because **each wavelength is refracted by a different amount** (violet most, red least).

Special detectors are needed for other waves: **antennas** (radio), **thermal imaging cameras** (infrared), **photographic film or digital detectors** (X-rays), **Geiger-Muller tubes** (gamma, ionising).
Objects appear coloured because they **reflect (or transmit)** some wavelengths and **absorb** others.
**Opaque** objects absorb or reflect light; **transparent** objects transmit it; **translucent** objects scatter it as it passes through.
The limited range of the eye is why **we cannot see** radio waves or infrared even though they carry energy.
core.h: Visible light and the human eye
core.p: **Visible light** is the only part of the EM spectrum that the human **eye can detect**, so we are only able to see a very **narrow range** of EM waves (about 400-700 nm). The different **colours** of light correspond to different wavelengths and frequencies, from **red (longest wavelength, lowest frequency)** to **violet (shortest wavelength, highest frequency)**. White light is a **mixture** of all the colours, and can be split by a prism because different wavelengths are **refracted by different amounts** in glass. Many animals detect different ranges: bees can see ultraviolet and some snakes sense infrared.

bullets: **Radio waves:** longest wavelength; **television, radio** (and wireless communication); can be absorbed by a conductor to make an **alternating current** (Higher tier detail in a later point).
**Microwaves:** **satellite communications** and **cooking**; can pass through the atmosphere, and are **absorbed by water molecules** in food, heating it.
**Infrared:** **electrical heaters, cooking food, infrared cameras**; given out by **warm objects**.
**Absorbed radio, microwave and infrared** mostly produces a **heating effect**.
**Microwaves** have wavelengths that can pass through the **atmosphere**, which is why they are suitable for communication with satellites.
**Infrared** is also used in **remote controls** and by **thermal cameras** to see warm objects in the dark.
Detail on uses and dangers is in the next point; here, link **region -> wavelength order -> typical effect**.
core.h: The regions of the spectrum: radio waves to infrared
core.p: **Radio waves** have the **longest wavelengths** and the lowest frequencies; they are used for **television and radio broadcasting** and are emitted by transmitters. **Microwaves** have shorter wavelengths and are used for **satellite communications and cooking food**. **Infrared (IR)** radiation is emitted by **all warm objects**; the hotter an object is, the more infrared it emits, and it is detected by **thermal imaging cameras** and felt by your skin as **heat**. In each case what matters for the exam is the **wavelength order**, the typical **source**, and the **effect when absorbed** (mostly **heating** for these three).

bullets: **Ultraviolet:** from the Sun; **sun tanning, energy-efficient lamps**; risks: **skin ageing, skin cancer, eye damage**.
**X-rays:** **medical imaging**; are **absorbed by dense materials (bone)** and pass through soft tissue; **ionising**.
**Gamma rays:** from the **nucleus** (radioactive decay); **medical imaging and treatments**; **ionising** and the most penetrating of the three.
The **ozone layer** in the atmosphere absorbs most **harmful ultraviolet** from the Sun.
X-rays and gamma rays are **hazardous** because they can **ionise** atoms in living cells.
**Radiographers** reduce risk by using **lead shielding** and limiting **dose and time of exposure**.
**Origin difference:** X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons lose energy (for example in an X-ray tube) or by changes in electrons in atoms; gamma rays come from the **nucleus**.
core.h: The regions of the spectrum: ultraviolet to gamma rays
core.p: **Ultraviolet (UV)** has a shorter wavelength than visible light and is emitted by the **Sun** and by special lamps; it can **cause sunburn**, **skin ageing and skin cancer**, and it makes some substances **fluoresce**. **X-rays** have shorter wavelengths again and pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense materials like **bone**, so they are used for **medical imaging**; they are **ionising**. **Gamma rays** have the shortest wavelengths and the highest frequencies and **originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom**; they are used in **medical treatments** (for example to kill cancer cells) and for sterilising equipment. X-rays and gamma rays are **ionising** and can **mutate genes and cause cancer**.

bullets: **Absorbed:** the wave's energy is transferred to the substance (for example **microwaves absorbed by water** heats food; **dark surfaces absorb infrared** and warm up).
**Transmitted:** the wave passes through (for example **visible light through glass**, **X-rays through soft tissue**, **radio waves through the walls of a house**).
**Reflected:** the wave bounces off a surface (for example **radio waves reflecting off the ionosphere**, light off a mirror, **metal surfaces reflect microwaves**).
**Refracted:** the wave changes direction as it changes speed on entering a different medium.
**Ultraviolet** is absorbed by **skin and glass**; **gamma** is only reduced by **thick lead or concrete**.
Examples must always say **which wavelength/part of the spectrum** and **which substance**.
Link to **required practical (reflection and refraction)**: investigating light reflecting and refracting is a model for all EM waves.
core.h: How different substances treat EM waves (absorb, transmit, reflect, refract)
core.p: When an EM wave meets a substance, it may be **absorbed**, **transmitted** (pass through), **reflected** or **refracted**, and **what happens depends on the wavelength** and on the material. For example, **glass transmits visible light** but **absorbs most ultraviolet**, a **metal reflects** radio waves and light, **bone absorbs X-rays** but soft tissue transmits them, and **water absorbs microwaves**. Because the behaviour changes with wavelength, different parts of the spectrum have different **uses** and **hazards**, and this is why we **choose a particular wavelength** for a particular job.

bullets: **Frequency** is **unchanged** at a boundary; **speed and wavelength** both decrease on entering glass.
**Air to glass:** light slows down (about 3.0 x 10^8 to about 2.0 x 10^8 m/s) and bends **towards the normal**.
**Glass to air:** speeds up and bends **away from the normal**.
At **90 degrees** to the surface (along the normal) there is **no change of direction**, but speed and wavelength **still change**.
**Violet** light is refracted **more** than red because it slows down more in glass.
Higher tier: **explain** the bending using the **change in speed** of the wave (wavefronts hit the boundary at different times).
Not all EM waves are refracted by the same materials in a useful way: for example, X-rays pass through glass with very little bending.
core.p: When an EM wave moves from one medium into another, its **speed changes**, and this causes **refraction** (change of direction) if it enters at an angle. Because the wave equation still applies, and the **frequency stays the same** (it is set by the source), the **wavelength changes** in proportion to the speed. On entering a **denser transparent medium** such as glass, light **slows down**, the **wavelength gets shorter**, and the ray **bends towards the normal**. On leaving, it speeds up again and bends away from the normal. Different wavelengths slow down by different amounts, so each is refracted by a slightly different amount, which is why a prism **splits white light**.

bullets: **Electrons moving between energy levels** emit or absorb EM waves (visible light and nearby ranges).
**Nuclear changes** (radioactive decay) give out **gamma rays**.
Very **hot** objects emit radiation across the spectrum; the hotter, the more and the **shorter the wavelength** of the peak.

**Radio waves** are produced by **alternating currents** in transmitters (oscillating electrons), and absorbed by aerials, creating an alternating current of the **same frequency** (Higher tier, covered in another point).
The **source** is where the energy comes from and the **absorber** is where it is delivered, matching the specification wording.
This links to **atomic structure** in Paper 1 (energy levels, nuclear decay).
Different processes give different parts of the spectrum, which is why **gamma rays** are linked to the **nucleus** rather than electrons.
core.h: How EM waves are produced and absorbed (link to atoms and nuclei)
core.p: EM waves are produced when **charged particles change their motion or energy**. **Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms** can result in EM waves being **generated or absorbed over a wide range of frequencies**. When an **electron** in an atom moves to a lower energy level it **emits** EM radiation (such as visible light or ultraviolet), and when radiation is absorbed an electron can move to a higher energy level or even leave the atom. **Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus** of an atom, for example after radioactive decay. Higher tier students also need to know that **radio waves** can be produced by **oscillations in electrical circuits**.

bullets: **Visible light and radio waves** reach the surface easily, so we can see and receive radio.
**Ozone** absorbs a large fraction of harmful **UV** from the Sun.
**X-rays and gamma rays** from space are **absorbed by the atmosphere**, protecting life but requiring **satellite observatories**.
**Infrared** is partly absorbed by greenhouse gases (**greenhouse effect**).
**Microwaves** pass through the atmosphere, which is why **satellite communications** use them.
Using different parts of the spectrum to observe the universe gives **different information** about stars and galaxies.
Link: this is another example of **different wavelengths being absorbed or transmitted differently**.
core.h: The atmosphere and the Sun: which waves reach us
core.p: The Sun emits radiation across the spectrum, but the **atmosphere absorbs some wavelengths and transmits others**. Most **visible light**, **radio waves** and some **microwaves** pass through to the ground, while most **ultraviolet is absorbed by the ozone layer**, and most **X-rays and gamma rays are absorbed** high up. Some infrared is absorbed by gases such as **carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour**, which links to the **greenhouse effect** in a later point. Telescopes for X-rays and gamma rays must therefore be placed on **satellites above the atmosphere**.

bullets: Know the **order** and be able to put any three groups in order of frequency or wavelength.
Know the **unit conversions** and write answers in **standard form** where needed.
**Describe** the property (transverse, energy transfer, same speed) then **explain** with 'because'.
**Compare** two waves by wavelength, frequency, energy, and penetration or ionising ability.
Link to **sound waves** (longitudinal, needs a medium, much slower) to highlight differences.
Link to **radioactivity** (gamma rays) and **the atmosphere**.
Use **data from a spectrum diagram** to read wavelengths for visible light.
core.p: This point is tested both as short recall (order, speed, transverse) and as a calculation with c = f λ. Higher tier questions may ask you to **explain why the wavelength changes** on refraction or to link **frequency to energy and danger**. Practise reading ranges from a labelled spectrum diagram and converting between nm, m, MHz and Hz. Use the precise terms **source**, **absorber**, **transverse**, **continuous spectrum** and **ionising** to match the mark scheme.

exam: **Name/Order (1-2 marks):** write the groups in order, for example 'radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma' and be clear which end is **long wavelength / low frequency**.
**State a property (1 mark):** 'All EM waves are **transverse**' or 'all travel at the **same speed in a vacuum**'. Use exact wording: **transverse**, **same speed**, **vacuum**.
**Calculation (3 marks):** write **c = f x λ** (or rearrange), substitute with values in **standard form**, then answer with the **unit** (m or Hz). Marks: equation / substitution / answer with unit.

**Explain why the wavelength changes on refraction (2-3 marks, Higher tier):** **speed changes** at the boundary; **frequency is constant** (set by the source); so v = f λ means the **wavelength changes** in proportion to the speed.
**Compare two waves (2-3 marks):** use **comparative words**: 'higher frequency, shorter wavelength, more energy'. Do not just describe each separately.
**Why one wave is suitable for a job (3 marks):** link a **property** (wavelength, penetration, absorption) to the **use** with a 'because'.
**Dangers question:** name the **type**, say it is **ionising**, and state the **effect** (cell damage, mutation, cancer for X-rays/gamma; skin cancer and ageing for UV).
**Graph/diagram questions:** read the spectrum on a **log scale** carefully; check whether the axis shows **wavelength** or **frequency**, as the direction is reversed.
**Six-mark questions:** structure by **moving through the spectrum** (properties, then uses, then hazards) and link each to wavelength or frequency.
**Key phrases:** 'transverse', 'transfer energy from the source to the absorber', 'continuous spectrum', 'same speed in a vacuum', 'ionising radiation', 'detected by the eye'.

mistakes.r: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.0 x 10^8 m/s); they differ in frequency and wavelength.
mistakes.w: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy.

mistakes.r: EM waves can travel through a vacuum; sound waves need a medium.
mistakes.w: EM waves need a medium to travel through.

mistakes.r: Higher frequency means SHORTER wavelength, because wave speed is constant (c = f x wavelength).
EM waves are transverse; the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
mistakes.w: EM waves are longitudinal like sound.

mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.
mistakes.w: The frequency of light changes when it enters glass.

mistakes.r: Only the high-frequency ones (UV, X-rays, gamma) are ionising; radio waves are safe at normal intensities. The risk depends on type of radiation and dose.
Infrared cannot be seen; the eye detects only visible light. We feel infrared as heating.
mistakes.w: Infrared is visible because it makes you feel warm.

mistakes.r: EM radiation includes harmless types like radio waves and light. Only some radiation (ionising) is from radioactive sources.
The spectrum is continuous: there are no gaps, and the groups overlap at their edges.
mistakes.w: The EM spectrum has gaps between the types.

summary: The specification asks you to know that EM waves are transverse waves that transfer energy from a source to an absorber, forming a continuous spectrum (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma, in order of increasing frequency), all travelling at the same speed in a vacuum, with the eye detecting only visible light and different substances absorbing, transmitting, reflecting or refracting each wavelength differently. It matters because it underpins communications, medicine, astronomy and radiation safety, and it is tested with the wave equation c = f x wavelength.

terms.d: A transverse wave that transfers energy from a source to an absorber and can travel through a vacuum.
The continuous range of EM waves grouped by wavelength and frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave (for example crest to crest), measured in metres.
The number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.
A region with no particles (empty space); EM waves can travel through it.
The speed of all EM waves in a vacuum, about 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
EM waves with the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies; used for television and radio.
EM waves used for satellite communications and cooking food.
EM radiation emitted by all warm objects, used in heaters, cooking and thermal imaging.
The only part of the EM spectrum detected by the human eye, from red to violet.
EM waves with shorter wavelengths than visible light; can cause skin ageing and skin cancer.
High-frequency EM waves used in medical imaging; ionising radiation.
The shortest-wavelength, highest-frequency EM waves, originating from the nucleus of an atom; ionising.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, which can damage cells and cause cancer.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another because its speed changes.
To take in energy from a wave so the energy is transferred to the substance.

worked.q: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 1.0 x 10^8 Hz (100 MHz). Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. The speed of EM waves is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. (3 marks)
steps: Write the equation: wave speed = frequency x wavelength, so wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.

worked.ans: Frequency = 5.5 x 10^14 Hz (to 2 significant figures; 5.45 x 10^14 Hz to 3 s.f.).
worked.q: Green light has a wavelength of 550 nm. Calculate its frequency. (3 marks)
steps: Convert the wavelength to metres: 550 nm = 550 x 10^-9 m = 5.5 x 10^-7 m.

worked.ans: Model answer: X-rays have a higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) than radio waves, so they carry more energy. This means X-rays are ionising radiation and can knock electrons out of atoms in cells, damaging DNA and causing mutations that may lead to cancer. Radio waves have much lower frequency and energy, so they are not ionising.
worked.q: Explain why X-rays are more dangerous to human cells than radio waves. (3 marks)
steps: Compare frequency: X-rays have a much higher frequency (shorter wavelength) than radio waves.
Link to energy: higher frequency radiation carries more energy.
Consequence: X-rays are ionising, so they can remove electrons from atoms, damaging cells and DNA (gene mutation, which may lead to cancer); radio waves are not ionising.
